name: Infrastructure Cost
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: The Hardware Behind the Ledger: What It Takes to Run a Node
lesson.summary: Infrastructure cost is the baseline expense of storage, compute, and bandwidth needed simply to run a synchronized node, separate from what a business pays per transaction, and it grows quickly once a company needs redundant, production-grade nodes.
lesson.body:
Infrastructure cost is the expense of the physical and network resources required just to participate in a blockchain as a node, separate from the fees paid for any individual transaction. Recall that a node, as covered earlier, is a computer running the blockchain's software, storing some or all of its transaction history, validating new blocks against the network's rules, and communicating with other nodes to stay synchronized. None of that happens for free. A node needs storage to hold the blockchain's data, which for a long-running, heavily used chain can grow to hundreds of gigabytes or more, processing power to validate incoming transactions and blocks, memory to keep recent state readily accessible, and a reliable, reasonably fast internet connection to stay in sync with the rest of the network, since the whole point of network fundamentals like peer-to-peer propagation is that a node has to actually receive and relay data continuously.

For an individual enthusiast, infrastructure cost might mean a single machine running in a closet, a cost measured in a modest electricity bill and the price of a hard drive. For a business that wants reliability, though, the calculus changes considerably. Running a node that a company's own application depends on for correctness, not just curiosity, generally means running it with redundancy, a backup node ready to take over if the primary fails, monitoring to catch problems before they cause an outage, and enough bandwidth headroom to handle traffic spikes without falling behind the rest of the network. Falling behind matters because a node that cannot keep up with new blocks stops being a reliable source of current information, which defeats the purpose of running it. Multiply a single node's costs by the number of nodes needed for redundancy, and infrastructure cost for a serious production deployment becomes a genuine budget line, not an afterthought.

It is worth being specific about what infrastructure cost does and does not include, since it is easy to conflate with the other cost categories already discussed. It is not the electricity spent competing to mine new blocks, that is computational cost. It is not the fee paid to have a specific transaction included in a block, that is transaction cost. Infrastructure cost is the baseline expense of simply having a working, synchronized copy of the network running and available, which a business incurs whether or not it submits a single transaction that day. A company could run a fully synced node for a month, pay nothing in transaction fees because it never actually submitted anything, and still have incurred real infrastructure cost the entire time.

This baseline expense is exactly what creates the decision explored next: does a business buy and maintain its own physical servers to run these nodes, or does it rent that capacity from a cloud provider instead. That choice, covered under cloud versus on-premise, is essentially a decision about who bears infrastructure cost and in what form, since the underlying requirement, a working node kept in sync with the network, does not go away either way.
